title: Slow Gaza reconstruction after the 2014 war and resignation as Deputy Prime Minister (2015)
description: After the 50-day war between Israel and Hamas in the summer of 2014, Mustafa, then Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy in the consensus government, was put in charge of rebuilding the Gaza Strip and led the ministerial committee at the donors' conference for Gaza's reconstruction in Cairo in 2014 (WAFA). Reconstruction 'sputtered, in large part because of continued political wrangling between Abbas and Hamas over who controls Gaza', according to the Associated Press (via The Times of Israel), and the UN criticised the international community in February 2015 for failing to make good on its aid pledges. On 31 March 2015 a government spokesman said Mustafa had submitted his resignation for personal reasons; Mustafa did not comment on why he stepped down. He remained chairman of the Palestine Investment Fund's board from 2015.
key_facts: Head of Gaza reconstruction after the 2014 war; led the ministerial committee at the 2014 Cairo donors' conference
31 March 2015: resignation submitted, officially for personal reasons
AP: reconstruction stalled amid the Fatah–Hamas dispute over control of Gaza

title: Named in the Panama Papers as director of an offshore holding company (2016)
description: The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Panama Papers investigation profiled Mustafa, then chairman of the Palestine Investment Fund (PIF), as a director since March 2006 of the Arab Palestinian Investment (Holding) Company Ltd. (APIC Holding), founded in the British Virgin Islands in 1994 as the parent of the Arab Palestinian Investment Company (APIC), in which the PIF is one of the shareholders; APIC has been listed on the Palestine Exchange since 2014. Mustafa confirmed that he had sat on APIC's board since 2006 representing the PIF's shares, that he resigned as a director when he joined the government and rejoined in February 2016, and said that all his mandates 'are cleared with all competent authorities in accordance to the applicable laws in Palestine'. The ICIJ states that inclusion in its database does not suggest illegal or improper conduct. No proceedings against Mustafa were reported.
key_facts: Director of APIC Holding (British Virgin Islands) since March 2006, representing the PIF's stake (ICIJ)
Left the board while in government (2013–2015), rejoined in February 2016
Mustafa: mandates cleared with the competent Palestinian authorities; ICIJ: no wrongdoing implied

title: Promotion to the PLO Executive Committee at a Central Council session boycotted by several factions (2022)
description: On 6–7 February 2022 the PLO Central Council, convened by President Abbas for the first time since 2018, filled vacant seats on the PLO Executive Committee: Mustafa, Abbas's longtime chief economic adviser, took the seat left by Hanan Ashrawi, who had resigned, and Hussein al-Sheikh that of the late Saeb Erekat. Hamas and Islamic Jihad declined to attend, saying power-sharing reforms had to come first; other factions and figures, including the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, Ashrawi and Nasser al-Kidwa, criticised the session, and The Times of Israel reported that boycotting factions accused Abbas of 'packing the body with loyalists'. The session's stated aim was to fill positions vacated through age, death and resignation (Arab News).
key_facts: Elected to the Executive Committee by the Central Council, filling Hanan Ashrawi's seat
Hamas and Islamic Jihad refused to attend; the PFLP said the council was not a unifying body
Critics: consolidation of Abbas's control over the PLO

title: Designation as Prime Minister without national consensus (2024)
description: Abbas designated Mustafa on 14 March 2024, after the resignation of Mohammad Shtayyeh's government, amid US and international calls for a 'revitalized' Palestinian Authority that could also govern Gaza after the war. Hamas called the decision 'unilateral', taken without consulting it shortly after factional talks in Moscow, and said that 'forming a new government without national consensus only reinforces a policy of unilateralism and deepens division'; Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front and the Palestinian National Initiative also objected. Fatah replied by blaming Hamas for what had befallen Gaza since 'the Oct. 7 adventure'. The cabinet was approved by presidential decree on 28 March 2024 and sworn in on 31 March without a parliamentary vote of confidence, in the absence of a functioning Legislative Council (AMAN); according to The Media Line's sources, Fatah and other factions were also unhappy with the choice, while the US State Department said it would judge the government 'based on its actions'.
key_facts: Hamas: 'unilateral' designation that 'deepens division'
Fatah blamed Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack for Gaza's situation
Confidence granted by presidential decree, not by a parliamentary vote

title: Suspension of Al Jazeera in Palestinian Authority areas (January–May 2025)
description: On 1 January 2025 a ministerial committee of the ministries of culture, interior and communications, according to WAFA, suspended Al Jazeera's broadcasts and froze the work of its journalists, employees, crews and affiliated channels in PA areas 'until their legal status is rectified', accusing the network of broadcasting 'inciting material'. The PA called the measure temporary and said it followed a complaint by the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate. It came during clashes since December 2024 between PA security forces and armed groups in Jenin refugee camp, which Al Jazeera had covered; the network accused the PA of 'attempting to deter Al Jazeera from covering escalating events in the occupied Palestinian territories'. The UN human rights office asked the PA to 'reverse course and respect its international law obligations', Germany's foreign ministry called the move 'deeply worrying', and Reporters Without Borders called it 'an unacceptable act of censorship'; Hamas also opposed it. On 12 May 2025 Al Jazeera's Ramallah bureau chief announced that President Abbas had decided to lift the ban from the next day; the order had been issued by Attorney General Akram Khatib, according to The Media Line.
key_facts: Order of 1 January 2025 by a ministerial committee (culture, interior, communications), per WAFA
Criticised by the UN human rights office, Germany, RSF and the Foreign Press Association
Lifted from 13 May 2025 after a decision by President Abbas

title: Dispute with Israel over the withheld clearance revenues (2025–2026)
description: Under the 1994 economic protocol of the Oslo Accords (the Paris Protocol), Israel collects customs and other taxes on goods destined for Palestinian areas and transfers them to the PA; these 'clearance revenues' make up about 60% of the PA's income according to The Times of Israel, 68% according to the PA cabinet. Since 2019 Israel has deducted amounts equivalent to the PA's payments to prisoners and families of those killed, and since November 2023 the sums the PA allocated to Gaza. From 2025 Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich froze the remaining transfers; his ministry said they had been frozen 'due to the minister's policy not to transfer funds to the Palestinian Authority in light of its actions against the State of Israel in the international arena and its support for incitement to terrorism'. In April 2026 it deducted about NIS 590 million of the NIS 740 million collected to pay PA debts to the Israel Electric Corporation and water utilities and froze the rest. Mustafa said on 26 April 2026 that 'not a single shekel of tax revenues has been transferred to us' in the past year, 'in an attempt to destroy the institutions of the State of Palestine'; Finance Minister Estephan Salameh put the withheld sum at about NIS 13 billion in February 2026. The Trump administration pressed Israel to release the funds, according to The Times of Israel. Mustafa has asked donors for emergency budget support and proposed that, if the Paris Protocol arrangements break down, the international community back an independent Palestinian customs system and currency.
key_facts: Israel's Finance Ministry: transfers frozen over the PA's international actions and 'support for incitement to terrorism'
April 2026: NIS 590 million of NIS 740 million deducted for utility debts, remainder frozen
Mustafa: 'not a single shekel' transferred in a year
October 2026: PA cabinet says all clearance revenues withheld for more than a year and a half

title: Partial salaries, delayed school year and public-sector strikes (2025–2026)
description: With clearance revenues withheld, the PA has been unable to pay its more than 150,000 employees in full. In summer 2025 May salaries were paid only at the end of July, and on 7 September 2025 June salaries were paid at 50% with a NIS 2,000 minimum. At the end of August 2025 the Education Ministry postponed the start of the school year by a week for more than 600,000 pupils; Mustafa told the cabinet that 'the Palestinian economy has contracted by 30% over the past year' and, at an emergency session, that preparations for the school year had not been completed because of the economic situation. After an audio clip in which a speaker says 'the prime minister told the ministers that there are no salaries, no money' went viral, police arrested three people in Ramallah under a law on social-media incitement (The Times of Israel). In 2026 January salaries were paid late and limited to NIS 2,000, health workers went on strike from April, and in June the Finance Ministry again offered 50% of wages, promising the rest 'when financial resources allow'. AMAN's 2025 report says that shortened government working hours, adopted to keep spending within the budget, hurt health, education and social protection services. Israel's defence establishment warned that the PA's financial distress could pose security risks, according to The Times of Israel.
key_facts: September 2025: school year postponed; June salaries paid at 50%
September 2025: three arrests over a viral audio clip about unpaid salaries
April–June 2026: strikes by health workers; 50% wage payment in June
20 October 2026: Finance Ministry still arranging a salary payment

title: Payments under the old prisoner system and dismissal of the finance minister (2025–2026)
description: After President Abbas's February 2025 decree replacing sentence-based payments to prisoners and families of those killed with needs-based assistance, a batch of payments was made under the old mechanism in November 2025. Finance Minister Omar al-Bitar, a member of Mustafa's cabinet, was then replaced by the planning minister, Estephan Salameh, without official explanation; Palestinian officials told The Times of Israel privately that an internal probe had found he approved stipends still tied to sentence length. Israel's foreign minister Gideon Sa'ar said the dismissal 'will not absolve' Abbas and the PA, which he accused of 'trying to fool the world'. In July 2026 the PA released the summary of an audit by Alvarez & Marsal that found the new programme largely separated from the old system, noting that the PA described the November payments as obligations accrued before the reform; the US State Department said the audit had not examined 'clandestine bypass channels' and accused the PA of trying to 'dupe' the international community, without presenting evidence, according to The Times of Israel. A Palestinian official described the Israeli campaign against the reform as part of an effort to bring about the PA's collapse. Mustafa is not a party to any proceeding in the matter.
key_facts: November 2025: payments under the old mechanism; Finance Minister Omar al-Bitar replaced by Estephan Salameh
July 2026: Alvarez & Marsal audit summary released; the State Department rejects it
Israel says payments continue; the PA says the old system has ended

title: Requirement for local election candidates to commit to the PLO programme (2025–2026)
description: Mustafa's Council of Ministers approved a new Local Council Elections Law in 2025 for the municipal elections of April 2026 (WAFA). According to the AMAN Coalition, amendments to the local elections law introduced controversial provisions, 'including a requirement that candidates sign a declaration committing to the political program of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), its international obligations, and internationally recognized resolutions'. AMAN reports that civil society and human rights organisations 'expressed strong reservations', arguing that such political conditions violate international human rights standards; it also criticised key laws on elections, parties and the constitution being issued by the presidency without sufficient national dialogue. Hamas did not formally take part in the elections and boycotted them in the West Bank, where many Fatah candidates ran unopposed. The PA presented the vote, including in Deir al-Balah in Gaza, as a step towards strengthening democratic life.
key_facts: Council of Ministers approved a new Local Council Elections Law (Mustafa, 20 November 2025)
Candidates required to commit to the PLO programme and its international obligations
Civil society and human rights groups objected (AMAN); Hamas did not formally take part

title: Senior appointments and promotions during austerity criticised by AMAN (2025)
description: In its report on 2025, published in 2026, the AMAN Coalition for Integrity and Accountability (the Palestinian chapter of Transparency International) recorded 84 appointments and 46 promotions in senior civilian and security posts and 41 appointments and promotions of ambassadors and consuls, 'despite government reform efforts aimed at reducing expenditures and restructuring the public sector', with about 30% of all promotions at the Palestinian Broadcasting Corporation. It said that some heads of institutions had been given ministerial rank outside job classifications, that factions continued to nominate ambassadors in exchange for accepting other appointments, and that people close to senior or former officials had been appointed to diplomatic posts, reflecting 'the persistence of patronage'. AMAN noted improvements in the procedure for appointing deputy ministers, and found institutions attached to the presidency the least transparent. Mustafa told donors in November 2025 that his government had 'introduced merit-based, competitive senior appointments'.
key_facts: 84 senior appointments and 46 promotions in 2025; 40 ambassadors and one consul appointed (AMAN)
AMAN: patronage and loyalty-based appointments persist; deputy-minister procedures improved
Mustafa: merit-based, competitive senior appointments introduced
